title: Effects of four workplace lighting technologies on perception, cognition and affective state
research_question: To examine the visual perceptual, affective, and cognitive implications of equipping temporary military shelters with either conventional fluorescent or advanced LED lighting systems with varied color temperature and luminance.

participants.description: 20 male and 4 female US Army infantry members, aged 18-30 years (Mean: 21.46, SD: 3.1), with normal visual acuity and color vision, stationed at the Natick Soldier Systems Center.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: A climate-controlled Tent Expandable Modular Personnel (TEMPER) military shelter (32' L x 20' 6" W, 640 sq. ft.) insulated for complete darkness, maintained at 70°F. Four lighting technologies were installed on separate days.
Fluorescent lighting technology with an average color temperature of 3345 K (range 3320-3370 K) and general shelter illumination of 20.3 foot candles.
LED 1 lighting technology with an average color temperature of 4175 K (range 4140-4210 K) and general shelter illumination of 17.8 foot candles.
LED 2 lighting technology with an average color temperature of 5448 K (range 5405-5490 K) and general shelter illumination of 22 foot candles.
LED 3 lighting technology with an average color temperature of 6029 K (range 5996-6062 K) and general shelter illumination of 32.6 foot candles.

mechanisms: Increased arousal from higher color temperature leads to faster reaction times in visual perception and cognitive tasks.
Positive moods (decreased depression, increased vigor/activity, decreased fatigue) induced by higher color temperatures predict enhanced cognitive performance.
Higher color temperatures mitigate symptoms similar to Seasonal Affective Disorder (SAD).
implementation_implications: LED technologies, particularly those with higher color temperatures, can promote increased alertness and visual cognitive efficiency among workers in industrial lighting applications.
Advanced lighting technologies can support positive mood, extended wakefulness, and speeded performance on visual perceptual and cognitive tasks.

tables.description: Mean tested color temperature of each lighting technology, in degrees Kelvin.

Mean and standard deviation for percent correct responses (Color Recognition Task 1), number of errors and completion times (Color Recognition Task 2), and error rates (Visual Acuity Task 1) for the three visual perception tasks and each of the four lighting conditions.
Mean and standard deviation composite mood difference (post-pre) scores for the depression, vigor/activity, and fatigue subscales of the POMS, for each of the four lighting conditions.
Mean and standard deviation accuracy and reaction times (RT in milliseconds) from each of the two primary cognitive tasks, and each of the four lighting conditions.

limitations: Participants were explicitly informed that the study was interested in how lighting variation influences affective state and cognition, which might have influenced results (though participants were blind to CCT manipulation and physical form factors).
Participants were only exposed to each lighting condition on one occasion, reducing the likelihood of expectations from preceding experiences influencing subsequent behavior.
Participants may have developed pre-existing preferences for certain lighting types from daily experiences, which could have influenced results.
